"Sir, my mocks have been stuck between 60 and 65 for a whole month," Zeenat said, dropping her bag on the desk.
"What have you been doing about it?" asked Akash.
"Adding topics. Every week a new one."
"And the old ones?"
"...Not touched."
"So what do you think is happening?"
"Maybe I'm collecting topics and forgetting them." She paused. "I'm going to stop adding. Two weeks on the weak chapters only, tests on those every third day."
"Sounds reasonable. What else?"
"Can you go over my test strategy? Which section I start with, when I skip."
Akash pulled out her last three papers. "Bring a pen. We'll look at the first ten minutes of each."

qa.q: How long had Zeenat's mocks been stuck?
qa.a: Zeenat's mocks had been stuck for a whole month.

qa.q: What is Zeenat feeling as she drops her bag on the desk?
qa.a: Zeenat feels frustrated and discouraged by the stalled scores, which comes out in the way she drops the bag and talks about the stall.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Zeenat try next if revision alone does not help, and why?
qa.a: She could take a shorter timed practice set on the weak chapters, because timed practice shows whether the problem is knowledge or speed.

qa.q: How does Akash see Zeenat's plateau?
qa.a: Akash asks questions instead of giving the answer and helps only with the test strategy, so Akash treats Zeenat as someone able to diagnose the problem.

grounding: Shows replanning after a plateau: stopping new topics, revising weak chapters and asking a teacher to review the test strategy.

subtype: Approach: adaptive replanning after a plateau [Revision]
passage: Last year my mock scores sat at 118 out of 200 for five straight weeks. I'm Nikita. I kept doing what I'd always done: a new chapter every two days, a mock every Sunday. Nothing moved. My friend Afreen said, "Maybe adding more isn't the answer." It annoyed me, because she was right. So I stopped. No new topics for two weeks. I went through my last six mocks and listed every chapter where I'd lost marks more than twice: ratios, seating puzzles, reading comprehension. Two weeks of only those. Then I took my test sheets to Mr. Khanna at the institute and asked him to watch how I attempted a paper. He noticed straight away that I did the hardest section first and panicked. "Start with English," he said. My next mock: 131. Looking back, the plateau wasn't telling me to work harder. It was telling me to work differently.

qa.q: What was Nikita's score for five weeks?
How did Nikita feel about Afreen's suggestion?
qa.a: Nikita felt annoyed at first, precisely because Afreen was right.

qa.q: What else could Nikita do if scores stall again?
qa.a: Nikita could repeat the same check: pause new topics, list repeatedly weak chapters, and ask a teacher to watch a timed attempt.
Mr. Khanna watched Nikita attempt a paper and spotted the panic from starting with the hardest section, giving a simple change.

grounding: Shows an aspirant whose mock scores stall stopping new topics, spending two weeks on weak chapters, and asking a teacher to review test strategy.

Coaching faculty note, Karthik (weekend batch), 14 October.
Karthik's mock scores have stayed between 142 and 146 out of 250 for four weeks, while he kept starting new units. Today he came to me with his friend Suraj and six marked test papers. He had already done something sensible on his own: he stopped adding topics last Monday and listed the chapters where he loses marks again and again. Geometry, data sufficiency and para-jumbles.
He asked me to look at his test strategy. I watched him attempt a sectional test. He spends too long proving each geometry answer instead of eliminating options, and leaves para-jumbles to the last five minutes.
We agreed: two weeks of only those three chapters, plus a rule to move on after ninety seconds. I'll review his next two mocks with him personally.
Update, 28 October: 158.

qa.q: Between which scores did Karthik's mocks stay?
How might Karthik have felt about four flat weeks?
qa.a: Karthik was probably frustrated and worried, which pushed him to stop adding topics and seek help.

qa.q: What else could Karthik do after the two weeks?
qa.a: He could keep a list of repeat-error chapters after every mock, so revision stays aimed at the real gaps.

qa.q: How does the faculty member see Karthik's first step?
qa.a: The faculty member sees it as sensible and builds on it, watching a test to find the strategy problem and agreeing a plan.

grounding: Illustrates an aspirant who, after a month of flat scores, stops new topics, revises weak chapters for two weeks and asks a teacher to review test strategy.
